name: Ts'ixa
catalog_citation: Fehn, Anne-Maria. 2016. A Grammar of Ts'ixa (Kalahari Khoe). PhD dissertation, Universitaet zu Koeln. KUPS eprint 7062 (380 pp.)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1.2 (PDF p. ~24, tone marking) and sec. 2.4 Tonology (pp. 45-46); sec. 10.1.3 Tonal profile
catalog_quote: Ts’ixa is a tone language and has three phonemic tone levels, which are marked as follows: á HIGH a MID à LOW ... 2.4 Tonology Tone in Ts’ixa is both lexically and grammatically distinctive. In this study, it is assumed that the tone-bearing unit is the mora, not the syllable. Hence, monosyllabic roots may be bimoraic and carry two register tones which together form a tonal melody (cf. Nakagawa 2006: 33). More research is needed to establish the number of distinct tone levels in Ts’ixa. Vossen (1997, 2013a) assumes two register tones, High and Low. However, this does not seem sufficient to cover the amount of tonal variation found in the present data. Measurements by means of Praat have yielded three tone levels – High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L). ... The following tonal melodies appear on bimoraic lexical roots: (1) HH ... (2) MM ... (3) LL ... (4) MH ... (5) HL ... (6) ML ... Tone in Ts’…

audit.reasoning: The coding (tonal; no word-stress rule stated; verdict TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT, domain UNSTATED) rests on the only reference grammar of Ts'ixa, Fehn's 380-pp Cologne dissertation (defended 2014, KUPS 2016), which we hold as the open KUPS PDF plus text layer; the deciding quotation is verbatim at sec. 2.1.2 (p. 23) and sec. 2.4 (p. 46), with sec. 10.1.3 (p. 293) restating three tone levels, and the full text contains zero occurrences of 'stress'. Glottolog lists no competing grammar or phonology. Two open follow-ups by the same author fetched sources now (Fehn & Phiri 2022 SPiL Plus 65:155; Fehn 2023 SAL 52 supp. 13:142) reaffirm a three-tone H/M/L register system and are silent on stress; the 2022 paper corrects some 2016 melody assignments (flip-flop on sandhi forms) but that does not touch the tonal-vs-stress classification. Only cosmetic locator drift (p. 23 not '~24'; p. 46 not '45-46'), alrea

sources.citation: Fehn, Anne-Maria. 2023. Is Ts’ixa (Kalahari Khoe) a dialect of Shua? A comparative take on nominal gender marking and alignment patterns. Studies in African Linguistics 52 (Supplement 13): 137-170. doi:10.32473/sal.52.supplement.13.133951 (open access)
sources.quote: 'if available, tone marking was included, but should be treated with caution, as a reliable analysis of tonal melodies and sandhi is presently only available for Khwe and Ts’ixa (Kilian-Hatz 2008, Fehn 2019, Fehn & Phiri 2022).' Morphosyntax paper; silent on stress, treats Ts'ixa as tonal.

sources.citation: Fehn, Anne-Maria & Admire Phiri. 2022. Juncture-Verb Constructions in Northeastern Kalahari Khoe: a comparative perspective. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 65(1): 147-190. doi:10.5842/65-1-973 (MPG PuRe public postprint)
sources.quote: 'Like Gǀui (Nakagawa 2006), Khwe (Fehn 2019, Kilian-Hatz 2008, Köhler 1981), Naro (Visser 2013) and presumably most Kalahari Khoe languages, Ts’ixa has a three-tone system of H(igh) vs. M(id) vs. L(ow).' ... 'A previous study overlooked that it is not uncommon for flip-flop to operate on sandhi forms, contributing to the partly erroneous tonal analysis published in Fehn (2016).' No mention of word stress anywhere (grep 'stress' = 1 hit, the verb 'stressing the need').
